title: Hop along the number line: add and subtract integers
description: Pick a start, choose add or subtract, pick a number, and watch the marker hop along a number line.
objective: Add and subtract positive and negative integers on a number line, see subtraction as adding the inverse, and check answers by estimating.
procedure_steps: Predict where the marker will land.
Choose a start, Add or Subtract, and a number.
Watch which way the marker hops.
observation: Write the expression and the place the marker landed for three different settings.
result: Adding a positive number moves the marker right and adding a negative number moves it left. Subtracting a number gives the same result as adding its inverse.
safety_instructions: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.
teacher_instructions: Ask students to predict before moving the sliders. Highlight that subtracting a negative moves the marker right.
student_instructions: Say the expression out loud before you check the answer.

observations.text: Adding or subtracting 0 changes nothing: the marker stays on {result}.
{start} + ({k}) = {result}: adding a positive number moves the marker right.
{start} + ({k}) = {result}: adding a negative number moves the marker left.
{start} - ({k}) = {result}: subtracting a positive number moves the marker left.
{start} - ({k}) = {result}: subtracting a negative is adding its inverse, {negk}, so the marker moves right.

mission.scenario: A marker sits on a number line. You decide how far it hops and which way.
mission.task: Predict where it lands, then test it.

predict.question: The marker starts at 3. You add -5. Where does it land?

instructions: Switch between Add and Subtract and change the number.
do.safety: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.

observe.prompt: Which way did the marker hop, and where did it land?

explain.text: The marker moves along the number line.

cases.text: Subtracting a number is the same as adding its inverse: a - b = a + (-b).
Adding a positive number moves right. Adding a negative number moves left.

concept.text: Integers are positive numbers, negative numbers and zero.
points: Positive numbers are right of 0 and negative numbers are left of 0.
To estimate, round first: 48 - 19 is about 50 - 20 = 30.

options.feedback: That treats it as -4 + -6. Subtracting a negative moves right.
Check the direction: subtracting a negative moves the marker right.

prompts: Which move surprised you most? Explain why in one sentence.

outcomes: Add and subtract integers on a number line.
Explain subtraction as adding the inverse.

title: Groups of signs: multiply and divide integers
description: Build groups of dots to see why the sign of a product depends on the signs of the factors, and check division with multiplication.
objective: Multiply and divide integers using the sign rules, see multiplication as repeated groups, and see division as the inverse of multiplication.
procedure_steps: Switch to Divide and check the answer.
observation: Record the signs of the two numbers and the sign of the answer for four settings.
result: Same signs give a positive product and different signs give a negative product. Dividing undoes multiplying, and dividing by 0 is not allowed.
safety_instructions: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.
teacher_instructions: Let students find the sign pattern themselves before you state it. Ask why dividing by 0 has no answer.
student_instructions: Look at the colour of the dots: red means a negative result.

derived.label: Product divided by the second number

observations.text: You cannot divide by 0, so there is no answer.
{p} / ({b}) = {q}. Check: ({q}) x ({b}) = {p}, so division undoes multiplication.
({a}) x ({b}) = 0: anything times 0 is 0.
({a}) x ({b}) = {p}: the same signs make a positive product.
({a}) x ({b}) = {p}: different signs make a negative product.

mission.scenario: Dots come in groups. Red dots are a negative result and blue dots are positive.
mission.task: Find the sign rule for multiplying, then use it to divide.

instructions: Change both numbers and watch the dots.
Look at the colour and the answer.
Switch to Divide and check the answer.
do.safety: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.

observe.prompt: What do you notice about the signs of the numbers and the colour of the dots?

explain.text: The signs of the numbers decide the sign of the answer.

cases.text: Division is the inverse of multiplication: if (-3) x 4 = -12, then -12 / 4 = -3.
One negative number: the product is negative.
Two negatives or two positives: the product is positive.

concept.text: Multiplying is repeated addition, and the sign follows a pattern.
points: Same signs: positive. Different signs: negative.
Division is the inverse of multiplication.
Brackets keep the signs clear: (-2) x (-5) = 10.

options.feedback: Yes: one negative sign gives a negative answer, and 24 / 6 = 4.
Different signs give a negative answer.
That subtracts. Division asks how many 6s fit in 24.

prompts: Why do you think dividing by 0 has no answer?

outcomes: Use the sign rules for multiplication and division.
Explain division as the inverse of multiplication.

title: When do the markers meet? Lowest common multiple
description: Two rows of markers hop in steps of two different numbers. Find the first place they land together.
objective: Find multiples and common multiples of two numbers and identify the lowest common multiple by listing multiples.
procedure_steps: Predict where the rows first meet.
observation: Write the two numbers and the first common multiple for four pairs.
result: The first value that appears in both rows is the lowest common multiple (LCM). If the two numbers share no factor, it is their product.
safety_instructions: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.
teacher_instructions: Ask students to predict the meeting point before moving the sliders, then check it against the rows.
student_instructions: Look for the green markers: they are in both rows.

observations.text: Both rows are the same, so they meet straight away at {l}.
These numbers share no common factor, so they first meet at their product: {l}.
The markers first land together at {l}: {m} x {tm} = {l} and {n} x {tn} = {l}. That is the lowest common multiple.

mission.scenario: Two rows of markers hop along a line, one in steps of the first number and one in steps of the second.
mission.task: Find the first number where both rows land together.

predict.question: One row hops in 4s and the other in 6s. Where do they first land on the same number?

instructions: Try numbers that share no factor, like 5 and 7.
do.safety: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.

observe.prompt: Where is the first green marker? What do the two hop counts tell you?

explain.text: A common multiple is in both rows.

cases.text: With no common factor, the rows do not meet until the product of the numbers.
The first common multiple is the lowest common multiple. Later green markers are more common multiples.

concept.text: The lowest common multiple (LCM) is the smallest number both numbers divide into.
points: A multiple is in the times table of a number.
List multiples of each and find the first shared one.

apply.question: Challenge: one bus returns every 6 minutes and another every 8 minutes. They leave together. When are they next together?

options.label: 24 minutes
options.feedback: Yes: the LCM of 6 and 8 is 24.

options.label: 48 minutes
options.feedback: 48 is a common multiple but not the first.

options.label: 14 minutes
options.feedback: Adding the numbers does not give a common multiple.

prompts: When would the LCM equal one of the two numbers?

outcomes: List multiples and find common multiples.
Find the LCM of two numbers.

title: Equal groups: find the highest common factor
description: Split two totals into equal groups of the same size and find the biggest group size that leaves nothing over.
objective: Find common factors and the highest common factor of two numbers using equal groups, and use the HCF to simplify a fraction.
procedure_steps: Change the two totals and the group size.
Find the biggest size that leaves none over for both.
observation: Write the group sizes that left nothing over for both totals, and the largest of them.
result: A group size that leaves nothing over for both totals is a common factor. The biggest one is the highest common factor (HCF).
safety_instructions: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.
teacher_instructions: Have students find all the common factors before naming the HCF. Link the HCF to simplifying a fraction.
student_instructions: A tick means equal groups. A cross means some are left over.

observations.text: {g} is the highest common factor of {a} and {b}. So {a}/{b} simplifies to {sa}/{sb}.
{g} is a common factor, but a bigger one works too: the highest is {h}.
{a} splits into equal groups of {g}, but {b} leaves {rb} over, so {g} is not a common factor.
{b} splits into equal groups of {g}, but {a} leaves {ra} over, so {g} is not a common factor.
{a} leaves {ra} over and {b} leaves {rb} over, so {g} is not a common factor.

mission.scenario: You have two piles of counters and want to share each into equal groups of the same size.
mission.task: Find the biggest group size that works for both piles.

predict.question: Can 24 and 36 both be split into equal groups of 6, with none left over?

instructions: Change the totals and the group size.
Look for a tick on both rows.
Find the biggest size that gets a tick on both.
do.safety: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.

observe.prompt: Which group sizes get a tick on both rows? Which is the biggest?

explain.text: Equal groups mean the group size is a factor.

cases.text: Both totals split into equal groups, so this size is a common factor of both.
Something is left over, so this size is not a factor of both totals.

concept.text: The highest common factor (HCF) is the largest factor shared by two numbers.
points: A factor divides a number exactly.
Divide the top and bottom of a fraction by the HCF to simplify it.

apply.question: Challenge: what is the HCF of 18 and 30, and what does 18/30 simplify to?

options.label: HCF 3, fraction 6/10
options.feedback: 3 is a common factor but not the highest, so 6/10 is not fully simplified.

prompts: How can the HCF help you simplify a fraction quickly?

outcomes: Find common factors using equal groups.
Find the HCF and use it to simplify a fraction.

title: The divisibility lab: test it, then check the rule
description: Choose a number and a divisor, make a guess, and watch the digit rule decide.
objective: Use the tests for divisibility by 2 to 11 to decide whether a number divides exactly, and explain why the test works.
procedure_steps: Choose a number and a divisor.
Make a guess, then read the rule on the tiles.
observation: For five numbers, write the divisor, the rule you used and whether you were right.
result: Each divisor has a quick test on the digits. The tiles show the rule, and the remainder confirms it.
safety_instructions: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.
teacher_instructions: Ask students to guess first, then use the highlighted tiles. Discuss why the digit-sum rule works for 3 and 9.
student_instructions: The gold tiles are the digits the rule looks at.

observations.text: Correct! {n} is divisible by {d}: the remainder is {r}.
Correct! {n} is not divisible by {d}: it leaves a remainder of {r}.
Not quite: {n} is divisible by {d}, with remainder {r}. Check the rule on the tiles.
Not quite: {n} is not divisible by {d}, with remainder {r}. Check the rule on the tiles.

mission.scenario: Each divisor has a quick digit test, so you do not need long division.
mission.task: Guess, then let the digit rule decide.

instructions: Pick a number and a divisor.
Switch the guess on or off, then check the result.
do.safety: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.

observe.prompt: Which digits did the rule use? Was your guess right?

explain.text: A number divides exactly when the digit rule says so.

cases.text: The rule gives a multiple of the divisor, so the number divides exactly.
The rule does not give a multiple of the divisor, so there is a remainder.

concept.text: A number is divisible by another when it divides with no remainder.
points: By 2, 5 or 10: look at the last digit.
By 4 or 8: look at the last two or three digits.
By 11: add and subtract the digits in turn.

options.label: Yes: the digit sum 12 is a multiple of 3
No: it ends in 5
options.feedback: The last digit matters for 2, 5 and 10, not for 3.

options.label: Only if it is even
options.feedback: Evenness is the rule for 2, not for 3.

prompts: Which rule is quickest for you? Why?

outcomes: Explain why a divisibility test works.

title: Squares and cubes: build them, then find the root
description: Build a flat square or a stack of layers from blocks and see how the side length is the root.
objective: Relate square and cube numbers to their roots using blocks, and estimate the root of a number that is not a perfect square or cube.
procedure_steps: Choose Square or Cube and a number.
Check whether the blocks fit exactly.
observation: Write three perfect squares, three perfect cubes and one number that is neither, with its estimated root.
result: A perfect square fills a square array and its side is the square root. A perfect cube fills a cube of layers and its edge is the cube root. Other numbers leave blocks over and their root lies between two whole numbers.
safety_instructions: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.
teacher_instructions: Let students find the perfect squares and cubes themselves, then discuss the leftover blocks for the other numbers.
student_instructions: Grey blocks are the ones left over.

observations.text: {v} = {r} x {r}, so the square root of {v} is {r}. A perfect square!
{v} = {r} x {r} x {r}, so the cube root of {v} is {r}. A perfect cube!
{v} is not a perfect square. {r} x {r} = {rp} is too small and {r1} x {r1} = {nextp} is too big, so the square root is between {r} and {r1}.
{v} is not a perfect cube. {r} cubed = {rp} is too small and {r1} cubed = {nextp} is too big, so the cube root is between {r} and {r1}.

mission.scenario: Blocks can make a square or a cube. The length of one side tells you the root.
mission.task: Find which numbers fit exactly and estimate the rest.

predict.question: What is the square root of 49?

instructions: Pick Square, then change the number.
Switch to Cube and try 8, 27 and 64.
Try a number that is not perfect and read the estimate.
do.safety: Nothing physical is handled in this virtual activity.

observe.prompt: Which numbers made a perfect fit? Which left blocks over?

explain.text: The root is the side of the shape that fits.

cases.text: The blocks fit exactly, so the root is a whole number.
Blocks are left over, so the root is not a whole number. It lies between two whole numbers.

concept.text: Square roots and cube roots undo squaring and cubing.
points: A perfect square fills a square: 36 = 6 x 6.
A perfect cube stacks n layers of n x n: 27 = 3 x 3 x 3.
For other numbers, estimate between two whole numbers.

apply.question: Challenge: which of these is a perfect cube?

options.feedback: 30 is neither a perfect square nor a perfect cube.
36 is a perfect square (6 x 6), not a perfect cube.

prompts: How would you estimate the square root of 40?

outcomes: Relate squares and cubes to their roots.
Estimate roots of numbers that are not perfect.
